title: A brief review on the mental health for select elements of the built environment
review_question: To synthesize peer-reviewed research on the relationships of three disparate elements in the design of buildings (connection to nature, personal control, indoor air quality) with respect to mental health outcomes.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Articles included were from developed countries, due to differences in building construction styles across the world.

synthesis_conclusions: The built environment may impact occupant mental health through its effects on connection to nature, personal control, and indoor air quality.
Contact with the natural environment has physiological and psychological benefits, and reduced contact leads to negative mental health outcomes.
Occupant control in the built environment can alter mental health through direct pathways (e.g., prevention of environmental stressors) and indirect pathways (e.g., social connections).
Indoor air quality is connected to mental health, as particulate matter, malodorous irritants, and toxins have been shown to alter mental well-being.
Architects and engineers have opportunities to optimize building designs for mental health, including planned urban greenspace, personalized temperature control, and building ventilation.
Interdisciplinary research utilizing controlled experiments is needed to confirm causality and improve understanding of mechanisms.
evidence_gaps: Need for further longitudinal and interventional research studies to define the exact importance nature plays in the built environment.
Warranted common terminology on what images of nature and which views from windows are important, and how to measure if a built environment is near a greenspace.

Empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that reduced-stress environments are dependent on allowing individuals to physically manipulate their surroundings (furniture, lighting, temperature) is inconclusive.
The biological processes that promote negative mental health outcomes due to exposure to particulate pollutants are still unclear.
Research on malodorous pollutants often shows no correlations between pollutants and annoyance, mood, and stress, indicating a need for better measurement of impact.
Need for large real-life studies with long longitudinal design to understand the likely direction of causality between built environment and mental health.
Need for more controlled intentionally small sample-based longitudinal experiments.
Need for efficacy, effectiveness, and implementation studies to address the complexity of the situation.
More effort to control extraneous variables in the built environment (materials, climate, stressors) for strengthened understanding.
Expansion of research into post-occupancy alterations to identify how occupants alter the built environment in ways that prove important to mental well-being.
heterogeneity_sources: Confounding variables such as socioeconomic status, co-occurring mental health conditions, and genetics make it difficult to elucidate how natural environments improve mental health outcomes.
Interpersonal variations of olfactory sensory levels and non-standard reaction to smell make measurements of malodorous pollutants difficult.
limitations: Mental health disorders are complex and often comorbid, making it difficult to distinguish whether issues are due to built environment or other pathophysiological/social etiologies.
Lower socioeconomic groups have greater rates of mental illness and live in lower quality houses, leading to potential confounding.
The theory of social drift may explain converging and potentially confounded multifactorial etiology of mental illness.
Blurred understanding of the direction of causality (mental illness as cause or consequence of poor quality built environments).

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Global urbanization, combined with evidence of increased prevalence of mental illness in urban environments, highlights a need to investigate potential connections between the built environment and mental health. Previous research has shown that the built environment may impact occupant mental health through its effects on connection to nature, personal control and indoor air quality. Contact with the natural environment has physiological and psychological benefits; consequently, reduced contact or exposure leads to negative mental health outcomes. The control an occupant has in the built environment can alter the mental health of individuals through direct pathways, such as prevention of exposures to environmental stressors and indirect pathways, such as social connections to others. Indoor air quality is connected to the mental health of built environment occupants, as particulate matter, malodorous irritants and toxins have all been shown to alter mental well-being. Opportunities for architects and engineers to optimize building designs that improve occupant mental health include planned urban greenspace, personalized temperature control and building ventilation. To understand optimization targets, interdisciplinary research utilizing controlled experiments are needed to confirm causality and improve our current understanding of mechanisms underlying the association between the built environment and mental health.
